evidence: Most run.sh scripts follow a minimal pattern: check tool, (optional build), run main file, echo success. Rust/run.sh and Cpp/run.sh deviate significantly with nested if/else blocks, optional --test/--docs/--bench flags, and output directory creation — creating style islands within the runner family

Brainfuck/run.sh and Jock/run.sh are structural outliers: Brainfuck/run.sh checks Python packages and conditionally runs additional analysis scripts; Jock/run.sh does not run any code at all and instead prints documentation — breaking the implicit 'run.sh runs the simulation' contract of all sibling scripts
SQL/run.sh uses a multi-case DB detection pattern unlike any other run.sh in the collection — necessary for its use case but a notable structural divergence
Python/run.sh contains inline Python code via python3 -c '...' that instantiates a class and generates visualizations — a pattern not used in any other language runner
Shell/run.sh creates config.sh via heredoc if absent — a config generation pattern not used by any other language runner

status_dashboard.sh declares 'Compiled' as a category containing only Golang and 'Esoteric' containing only Brainfuck, while run_all.sh has no such categories — the category taxonomy exists in only one of the two top-level orchestration files

Naming: status_dashboard.sh uses show_header(), show_system_info(), show_statistics(), show_implementations(), show_recent_activity(), show_recommendations() — consistent show_ prefix convention. run_all.sh uses run_language(), show_usage(), list_languages() — mixed verb prefix convention across sibling orchestrators

strengths: All language runners share the same file name (run.sh) and location pattern, making discovery consistent
All runners use set -e and the same 'command -v <tool>' guard-clause idiom
All runners use the same emoji-prefixed echo style for status messages
The majority of runners (Ada, Erlang, Elixir, Haskell, Golang, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript) follow a compact 3-phase pattern: check, build, run
convention_outlier.issue_character: Convention drift is concentrated in a handful of outlier scripts (Rust, Cpp, Brainfuck, Jock, Python) that add significant structural complexity relative to their siblings, and in the two top-level orchestrators which apply different naming conventions to their functions.
convention_outlier.score_rationale: The shared file naming, set -e usage, guard-clause idiom, and echo style represent a strong base convention. However, Jock/run.sh breaks the 'run.sh actually runs something' contract held by all 38 other siblings, and Rust/run.sh and Cpp/run.sh introduce nested error-handling structures absent elsewhere. These are not minor style variations — Jock's deviation means a developer running './run.sh' in every language directory will get a documentation printout instead of a simulation for Jock, while the nested if-blocks in Rust and Cpp create a false impression that other runners also handle partial failures. This mixed picture warrants a score in the 70–75 range: mostly consistent with notable outliers that a developer would notice.

issues.summary: Jock/run.sh prints documentation instead of running simulation code, breaking the universal 'run.sh executes the implementation' contract of all 38 sibling scripts
evidence: Lines 25-48: the script prints instructions and documentation strings, never executing any simulation
All other run.sh scripts (Ada, Erlang, Elixir, Haskell, Golang, Java, JavaScript, C, Cpp, Rust, Python, etc.) execute the actual language implementation
issues.suggestion: Either implement a runnable Jock simulation stub that exits with an informative message about Urbit requirements, or rename the file to README_run_instructions.sh and create a proper run.sh that attempts execution and exits with a clear 'Jock requires Urbit' error message.

issues.summary: Language category groupings (Systems, Functional, Scripting, etc.) exist only in status_dashboard.sh — run_all.sh uses a flat uncategorized list, creating divergent mental models
evidence: status_dashboard.sh lines 150-158: declare -A categories with Systems, Functional, Scripting, Scientific, JVM, Logic, Esoteric, Compiled groupings
run_all.sh lines 21-61: flat LANGUAGES array with no categorization
status_dashboard.sh hard-codes numeric category counts (line 127-132) that are not derived from the categories array
issues.suggestion: Extract the categories associative array into a shared data file (e.g. Shell/language_registry.sh) and source it from both run_all.sh and status_dashboard.sh. Compute numeric counts from the data rather than hard-coding them.

issues.summary: status_dashboard.sh uses a consistent show_ verb prefix for all functions; run_all.sh uses mixed verbs (run_, show_, list_) with no consistent convention
evidence: status_dashboard.sh: show_header(), show_system_info(), show_statistics(), show_implementations(), show_recent_activity(), show_recommendations() — all show_
run_all.sh: run_language(), show_usage(), list_languages() — three different verb prefixes across three sibling functions in the same file
issues.suggestion: Standardize run_all.sh function names to use consistent prefixes matching their roles: run_language() is fine, rename show_usage() to print_usage() and list_languages() to print_language_list() for consistency with the action-oriented naming.

root_causes: The runner scripts were likely added incrementally as languages were added to the collection; early entries established a minimal pattern that later, more complex languages (Rust, Cpp) extended without refactoring siblings to match
The Jock implementation is inherently documentation-only (it requires an Urbit ship) but was placed in a run.sh file that developers would assume follows the execution contract
